decks.title: India's External Relations — Part 1: Non-Alignment and China
goals: Explain the international context in which India's foreign policy was shaped after 1947
Explain the objectives of foreign policy and the policy of non-alignment
Describe India's role in Afro-Asian unity and the Non-Aligned Movement
Analyse India–China relations up to and after the war of 1962

slides.heading: India's External Relations
slides.body_md: Part 1 — how a newly free India dealt with the **Cold War**, built **non-alignment**, and faced the **1962 war** with China.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: the world in 1947, Nehru and the goals of foreign policy, non-alignment, Afro-Asian unity, and India–China relations from friendship to war
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: In 1947 India became free in a world that was splitting into two rival camps. A new nation, poor but proud of its freedom struggle, had to decide how to deal with the great powers and with its neighbours. In this part we look at the goals of India's foreign policy, the idea of non-alignment, and the story of relations with China up to the war of 1962.

slides.heading: The world India entered

rows: Wave of decolonisation in Asia and Africa
Poverty and the need to rebuild
Need for aid, technology and peace
A stage for a new country's voice

visual.alt: Table of four features of the world in 1947 and what each meant for India: the Cold War meant pressure to take sides; decolonisation gave partners among new nations; poverty meant a need for aid, technology and peace; the new United Nations gave a stage

slides.narration: Four features of the world shaped India's choices. The Cold War pressed new nations to take sides. Many countries of Asia and Africa were winning freedom at the same time, so India had natural partners. India was poor and needed aid, technology and peace to develop. And the new United Nations gave a young country a place to make its voice heard.

slides.heading: Nehru and the goals of foreign policy
slides.body_md: Jawaharlal Nehru was **Prime Minister and Foreign Minister** from 1947 to 1964.
bullets: Preserve **sovereignty** won after a long struggle
Protect **territorial integrity**
Promote **rapid economic development**
Means: **non-alignment**
slides.narration: Nehru held both the post of Prime Minister and that of Foreign Minister, so he shaped foreign policy closely. His aims were to keep India's hard-won independence, to protect its territory, and to develop the economy quickly. The Constitution also asks the state to promote peace and respect for international law. The chosen method was non-alignment.

visual.caption: Non-alignment: outside both blocs, but not outside world affairs

slides.narration: Here is the idea in one picture. On one side is the Western bloc led by the United States, on the other the Eastern bloc led by the Soviet Union. India chose to join neither military alliance. Instead it judged each issue on its merits and dealt with both sides for aid and trade. Notice that India stays in the picture: it is outside the blocs, but not outside world affairs.

slides.heading: Quick check: non-alignment
slides.body_md: True or false? Non-alignment means the same as isolationism.
slides.narration: Think about whether India kept away from world affairs or took part in them.

slides.heading: Non-alignment is not neutrality

rows: No, keeps away from world affairs
No, stays out of disputes and wars

visual.alt: Table comparing non-alignment, isolationism, neutrality and alliance membership: only alliance members join a bloc; only non-alignment combines staying out of blocs with active positions on world issues
visual.caption: Non-alignment is not neutrality

slides.narration: Students often mix up three ideas. Isolationism means keeping away from world affairs altogether. Neutrality means staying out of wars and disputes. Non-alignment is different from both. India stayed out of military blocs, but it took positions, mediated in crises and supported freedom struggles. The best one-line answer is: out of blocs, active on issues.

slides.heading: Afro-Asian unity and the birth of NAM

visual.alt: Flow of Afro-Asian unity: the Asian Relations Conference in New Delhi in 1947, support to Indonesia, the Bandung conference in 1955 and the first NAM summit at Belgrade in 1961
visual.caption: From Afro-Asian solidarity to NAM

slides.narration: India reached out to other newly free nations. It hosted the Asian Relations Conference in March 1947, even before independence, and backed Indonesia's fight for freedom. In 1955 Asian and African states met at Bandung in Indonesia. In 1961 the first summit of the Non-Aligned Movement was held at Belgrade, led by Nehru, Tito, Nasser, Sukarno and Nkrumah.

slides.heading: Quick check: Bandung
slides.body_md: Name the Indonesian city where the Asian-African conference of 1955 was held.
slides.narration: This conference came six years before the first summit of the Non-Aligned Movement.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: is this non-alignment?
slides.body_md: Decide which policy an imagined country of 1956 is following.
bullets: Step 1 — Does it join a **military pact**? No.
Step 2 — Does it take **positions** on issues? Yes, criticising each superpower on different questions.
Step 3 — Does it deal with **both sides**? Yes, for aid.
Step 4 — Out of blocs plus active on issues: **non-alignment**.

rows: Criticises each superpower on different issues
Takes aid from both for dams and steel

visual.alt: Worked example table: an imagined country that refuses pacts, criticises each superpower on different issues, takes aid from both and joins conferences of new nations is following non-alignment
visual.caption: Verdict: non-alignment

slides.narration: Let us apply the idea. An imagined country refuses all pacts, criticises one superpower on one question and the other on another, and takes aid from both for its dams and steel plants. It is not isolationist, because it takes part. It is not neutral, because it takes positions. It is not a bloc member. So it is following non-alignment.

slides.heading: Debates and changes
bullets: Critics said non-alignment was **unprincipled** or tilted towards the **USSR**, especially after 1971.
The Janata government of **1977** promised **genuine non-alignment**.
After the Cold War, debate on whether NAM still matters.
slides.narration: Non-alignment had critics. Some said it avoided hard choices; others said India leaned towards the Soviet Union, especially after the treaty of 1971. When the Janata Party came to power in 1977, it said it would follow genuine non-alignment. After the Cold War ended, people asked whether the idea still had meaning. Exam answers should present such debates fairly, with arguments on each side.

slides.heading: India and China: a friendly start

rows: Panchsheel: five principles of peaceful coexistence
Close contacts and visits between leaders

visual.alt: Table of early friendship with China: recognition of the People's Republic in 1949 to 1950, Panchsheel in 1954 and visits between leaders in the 1950s

slides.narration: Relations with China began warmly. India was among the first countries to recognise the People's Republic. In 1954 the two signed an agreement based on Panchsheel, the five principles of peaceful coexistence: respect for each other's territory, non-aggression, non-interference, equality and mutual benefit, and peaceful coexistence. Leaders of both countries visited each other in the 1950s.

slides.narration: This timeline shows the arc of the relationship. Recognition in 1949 and Panchsheel in 1954 mark the friendly phase. The Dalai Lama's asylum in 1959 and the war of 1962 mark the break. Full diplomatic relations were restored in 1976, and Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi's visit in 1988 opened a new phase of contact.

slides.heading: Tibet and the boundary
slides.body_md: China took control of **Tibet** in 1950; in **1959** the Dalai Lama fled and India gave him **asylum**. The **boundary** was disputed in two sectors.

rows: North-East Frontier Agency, today Arunachal Pradesh

visual.alt: Table of the two main areas of the boundary dispute: Aksai Chin in the western sector and the North-East Frontier Agency, today Arunachal Pradesh, in the eastern sector
visual.caption: Rival claims on two sectors

slides.narration: Two issues strained the friendship. China took control of Tibet in 1950, and after an uprising in 1959 the Dalai Lama fled to India, which gave him asylum. China objected. At the same time the two sides had rival claims on the boundary: Aksai Chin in the western sector and the area then called the North-East Frontier Agency in the east.

slides.body_md: Arrange the events in India–China relations in the correct order.
slides.narration: Use the timeline: the agreement came first, the war in between, and normal ties later.

slides.heading: The war of 1962

nodes.label: Unsettled boundary and mistrust over Tibet

visual.alt: Flow of the 1962 war: an unsettled boundary and mistrust over Tibet, fighting in both sectors in October, reverses for Indian forces, and a unilateral ceasefire declared by China in November
visual.caption: The war in brief

slides.narration: In October 1962 fighting broke out in both sectors. Indian forces suffered serious reverses. In November China declared a unilateral ceasefire, and the fighting stopped. Describe the war factually: the causes were the unsettled boundary and the mistrust that had grown over Tibet.

slides.heading: Effects of the war

rows: Setback to national pride and to Nehru's standing
Sharp rise in spending; modernisation of forces
Defence Minister resigns; first no-confidence motion (1963)
Differences over China feed the CPI split (1964)

visual.alt: Table of the effects of the 1962 war: a setback to image and morale, a sharp rise in defence spending, the resignation of the Defence Minister and the first no-confidence motion in 1963, and differences that fed the split of the CPI in 1964

slides.narration: The war had several effects at home. It hurt national morale and Nehru's standing. Defence spending rose sharply and the forces were modernised. The Defence Minister resigned, and in 1963 the government faced its first no-confidence motion, which it survived. Differences over China also contributed to the split in the Communist Party of India in 1964.

slides.heading: Quick check: how the war ended
slides.body_md: True or false? The 1962 war ended when China declared a unilateral ceasefire.
slides.narration: Recall what happened in November 1962.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: planning a 5-mark answer
slides.body_md: Question: *Trace India–China relations from 1949 to 1962 and assess the main cause of the conflict.*
bullets: Step 1 — Four headed points in **time order**.
Step 2 — One fact or date in **each** point.
Step 3 — A **judgement** on the main cause, with a reason.
Step 4 — Neutral wording; about 100 words.

rows: Boundary: Aksai Chin and the eastern sector
The war of 1962 and the ceasefire
Your judgement on the main cause

visual.alt: Worked example table planning a 5-mark answer on India–China relations: early friendship, Tibet, the boundary, the war and a judgement on the main cause
visual.caption: Five headed points, one judgement

slides.narration: For a five-mark answer, plan five headed points. Write four points in time order: early friendship, Tibet, the boundary dispute and the war itself, each with a date. Then give a judgement on the main cause, with a reason. Keep the wording neutral and factual, and stay near a hundred words.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: Out of blocs, active on issues; NAM from 1961

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: goals of sovereignty, territorial integrity and development; non-alignment as staying out of blocs while active on issues; Afro-Asian unity; and India–China relations from 1954 to 1976

slides.narration: To sum up Part 1. India's foreign policy aimed at sovereignty, territorial integrity and development. Its method was non-alignment: out of blocs, active on issues. India built Afro-Asian unity and helped found the Non-Aligned Movement in 1961. With China, friendship and Panchsheel gave way to the war of 1962, and full relations were restored only in 1976.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Never define non-alignment as **neutrality** or **isolation**.
Learn the pairs: **Bandung 1955**, **Belgrade 1961**, **Panchsheel 1954**, **war 1962**.
For 1962, give **two causes** (boundary, Tibet) and **domestic effects**.
Keep wording **neutral** about China and all leaders.
Source parts: quote for "which line", name and explain for the rest.
slides.narration: A few tips. Never call non-alignment neutrality or isolation. Learn the key dates in pairs. For the 1962 war, give two causes and at least two effects inside India. Keep your wording neutral and factual. In source questions, quote exactly when asked for a line, and name and explain the concept elsewhere.

decks.title: India's External Relations — Part 2: Pakistan and Nuclear Policy
goals: Describe the conflicts and agreements between India and Pakistan from 1947 to 1999
Explain the wars of 1965 and 1971 and their outcomes
Explain the development of India's nuclear policy and its doctrine

slides.heading: Wars, peace and the bomb
slides.body_md: Part 2 — **India and Pakistan** from 1947 to 1999, and **India's nuclear policy**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: Kashmir and the Indus treaty, the 1965 war and Tashkent, the 1971 war and Simla, Kargil, and nuclear policy
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: In this part we turn to India's relations with Pakistan, a neighbour born from the same Partition. The two countries fought wars and also signed important agreements. Then we study how India's nuclear policy developed, from peaceful research in the 1940s to the tests of 1998 and the doctrine that followed.

slides.heading: Kashmir: the first conflict

rows: Fighting begins after raiders enter Kashmir; the ruler accedes to India
India takes the issue to the United Nations
A ceasefire line divides the territory

visual.alt: Table of the Kashmir conflict of 1947 to 1949: fighting and accession in 1947, India taking the matter to the United Nations in 1948, and a ceasefire line in 1949
visual.caption: The dispute that shaped the relationship

slides.narration: The conflict over Kashmir began soon after independence. In October 1947 armed raiders entered Kashmir and its ruler acceded to India; fighting followed. India took the matter to the United Nations, and in 1949 a ceasefire line divided the territory. The two countries have held conflicting positions on Kashmir ever since.

slides.heading: Cooperation on rivers

headers: Feature of the Indus Waters Treaty
rows: 1960; Prime Minister Nehru and President Ayub Khan
Sharing the rivers of the Indus system

visual.alt: Table of the Indus Waters Treaty: signed in 1960 by Nehru and Ayub Khan, mediated by the World Bank, on sharing the rivers of the Indus system

slides.narration: Conflict did not stop cooperation entirely. In 1960 Prime Minister Nehru and President Ayub Khan signed the Indus Waters Treaty, with the World Bank as mediator. It set out how the rivers of the Indus system would be shared. It is often cited as an example of practical cooperation between the two countries despite tension.

slides.heading: Why India stayed out of the treaties

rows: Five states keep weapons; others give up the option

visual.alt: Table of two treaties: the NPT of 1968 lets five states keep weapons while others give up the option, which India calls discriminatory; the CTBT of 1996 bans all test explosions, which India says freezes an unequal order
visual.caption: Why India stayed out

slides.narration: India rejected the Non-Proliferation Treaty as discriminatory. It allowed five states that had tested before 1967 to keep their weapons, while all others had to give up the option. India said it supported universal disarmament, not a permanent division between nuclear haves and have-nots. It took a similar view of the test ban treaty of 1996.

visual.caption: Two pillars of the declared doctrine

slides.narration: In May 1998 India carried out a series of tests at Pokhran, and Pakistan tested soon after. India then declared its doctrine. First, no first use: India would use nuclear weapons only to answer a nuclear attack. Second, credible minimum deterrence: India would keep only enough capability to make an attack unthinkable. India also says it remains committed to global disarmament.

sections.heading: 1. Context and objectives
sections.body_md:
India became independent in the early years of the **Cold War**, when many Asian and African countries were also gaining freedom. **Jawaharlal Nehru** was both Prime Minister and Foreign Minister from 1947 to 1964.

**Objectives:** keep the **sovereignty** won in the freedom struggle; protect **territorial integrity**; achieve **rapid economic development**.

The **Directive Principles** (Article 51) ask the state to promote international peace and security, just relations between nations and respect for international law.

A state's supreme authority to decide its own affairs without outside control.

rows: Wave of decolonisation in Asia and Africa
Poverty and the need to rebuild
Need for aid, technology and peace
A stage for a new country's voice

sections.heading: 2. Non-alignment and the Non-Aligned Movement
sections.body_md:
**Non-alignment** means keeping out of the military alliances of the two Cold War blocs while taking an **independent, active** part in world affairs. It is **not** isolationism and **not** neutrality.

**Afro-Asian unity:** Asian Relations Conference (New Delhi, **March 1947**); support for Indonesia's freedom; Asian-African conference at **Bandung (1955)**.

**NAM:** first summit at **Belgrade, 1961**; leaders usually named as founders: **Nehru, Tito, Nasser, Sukarno, Nkrumah**.

**Debates:** critics spoke of a Soviet tilt, especially after 1971; the **Janata** government (1977) promised *genuine non-alignment*; after the Cold War its relevance was debated.

key_terms.definition_md: Staying out of military blocs while judging each international issue independently.
Keeping away from world affairs altogether.
Staying out of wars and disputes, taking no side.

sections.heading: 3. India and China before 1962
sections.body_md:
- India recognised the **People's Republic of China** soon after its founding (1949).
- **Panchsheel (1954):** five principles of peaceful coexistence — mutual respect for territorial integrity and sovereignty, mutual non-aggression, non-interference in internal affairs, equality and mutual benefit, peaceful coexistence.
- **Tibet:** China took control in 1950; after the 1959 uprising the **Dalai Lama** came to India and received **asylum**, which China resented.
- **Boundary:** rival claims in the **western sector (Aksai Chin)** and the **eastern sector (NEFA, now Arunachal Pradesh)**.

sections.heading: 4. The war of 1962 and after
sections.body_md:
- Fighting in both sectors in **October 1962**; Indian forces faced reverses; China declared a **unilateral ceasefire** in **November**.
- **Effects in India:** blow to morale and to Nehru's standing; **defence spending raised** and forces modernised; **Defence Minister V. K. Krishna Menon** resigned; first **no-confidence motion** in the Lok Sabha (1963), which the government survived; differences over China contributed to the **CPI split (1964)**.
- **Normalisation:** full diplomatic relations restored in **1976**; Prime Minister **Rajiv Gandhi visited China in 1988**.

key_terms.definition_md: A halt in fighting announced by one side without a joint agreement.
A motion in the Lok Sabha asking whether the government still has the majority's support.

sections.heading: 5. Wars and peace with Pakistan
sections.body_md:
- **1947–48:** fighting in **Kashmir**; the ruler acceded to India; India took the matter to the **UN**; a **ceasefire line** in 1949. The two countries have held conflicting positions on Kashmir since.
- **Indus Waters Treaty (1960):** signed by **Nehru and Ayub Khan**, mediated by the **World Bank**.
- **1965:** Rann of Kutch clashes (April), larger offensive in **Jammu and Kashmir** (August–September); **UN-backed ceasefire**; **Tashkent Agreement** (January 1966) with **Soviet** mediation — forces returned to pre-war positions. PM **Lal Bahadur Shastri**.
- **1971:** Awami League (Sheikh Mujibur Rahman) won the 1970 elections; crackdown from **March 1971**; **millions of refugees** in India; **Indo-Soviet Treaty (August 1971)**; war in **December**; surrender at **Dhaka on 16 December**; **Bangladesh** independent.
- **Simla Agreement (July 1972):** Indira Gandhi and Zulfikar Ali Bhutto; peaceful, **bilateral** settlement; respect for the **line of control**.
- **1999:** Lahore bus journey (February); **Kargil conflict** (May–July).

key_terms.definition_md: The line in Jammu and Kashmir, confirmed at Simla, that separates the areas held by India and Pakistan.
Between two countries only, without a third party.

sections.heading: 6. India's nuclear policy
sections.body_md:
- **Beginnings:** programme under **Homi J. Bhabha** from the late 1940s, for peaceful uses; Nehru opposed nuclear weapons and pressed for **comprehensive disarmament**.
- **China's test (1964)** raised a security concern.
- **NPT (1968):** India stayed out, calling it **discriminatory** — it recognises only the five states that tested before 1 January 1967 as nuclear-weapon states.
- **May 1974:** first test at **Pokhran**, described as a *peaceful nuclear explosion*.
- **CTBT (1996):** not signed, on similar grounds.
- **May 1998:** tests at Pokhran; Pakistan tested later that month.
- **Doctrine:** **no first use** and **credible minimum deterrence**; continued support for global, non-discriminatory disarmament.

key_terms.definition_md: Preventing an attack by making the attacker expect an unacceptable response.
The Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty of 1996, banning all nuclear test explosions.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Calling non-alignment *neutrality* or *isolation*.
- Mixing up **Bandung (1955)** and **Belgrade (1961)**.
- Placing **Tashkent** after 1971 or **Simla** after 1965.
- Saying the Tashkent or Simla agreement settled Kashmir — neither did.
- Writing only "discriminatory" for the NPT without explaining why.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark MCQ and assertion-reason: one correct option.
- 2 marks: two points (30–50 words); 3 marks: three points (50–80 words).
- 5 marks: five headed points (80–120 words), with dates; evaluation questions need both sides and a judgement.
- Source-based (4 marks): quote exactly for "which line" parts; name and explain the concept for the rest.

**Neutral wording:** describe disputes as conflicting positions and events factually; avoid blaming any country or leader.

questions.stem_md: Which group of leaders is usually named as the founders of the Non-Aligned Movement?

options.text_md: Nehru (India), Churchill (Britain), Roosevelt (USA) and Stalin (USSR)
Nehru (India), Tito (Yugoslavia), Nasser (Egypt), Sukarno (Indonesia) and Nkrumah (Ghana)
Nehru (India), Mao (China), Ayub Khan (Pakistan) and Bandaranaike (Sri Lanka)
Nehru (India), de Gaulle (France), Adenauer (West Germany) and Tito (Yugoslavia)

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Nehru (India), Tito (Yugoslavia), Nasser (Egypt), Sukarno (Indonesia) and Nkrumah (Ghana). NAM grew from newly independent and non-bloc states; its first summit at Belgrade in 1961 was led by these five. The other sets include leaders of the two Cold War blocs or of countries outside the movement's founding group.

questions.stem_md: Where and when was the first summit of the Non-Aligned Movement held?

options.text_md: Bandung, 1955
New Delhi, 1947
Cairo, 1964
Belgrade, 1961

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Belgrade, 1961. The first NAM summit met in Belgrade in September 1961. The Bandung Conference of 1955 was the Asian-African conference that prepared the ground; New Delhi hosted the Asian Relations Conference in 1947.

questions.stem_md: The Asian-African conference held at Bandung, Indonesia, in 1955 is remembered mainly because it

options.text_md: brought newly independent Asian and African states together and prepared the ground for the Non-Aligned Movement
set up the United Nations Security Council
created a military alliance of Asian states against the Soviet Union
ended the Korean War by a peace treaty

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** brought newly independent Asian and African states together and prepared the ground for the Non-Aligned Movement. Bandung marked Afro-Asian solidarity against colonialism and racial discrimination and led towards NAM. It created no alliance, had nothing to do with founding the Security Council, and did not end the Korean War.

questions.stem_md: Which statement best describes India's policy of non-alignment in the 1950s?

options.text_md: Staying away from all world affairs, like a country that keeps to itself
Remaining neutral in every dispute, including wars of independence
Staying out of both Cold War military blocs while taking an active, independent stand on world issues
Joining the US-led bloc for aid and the Soviet bloc for arms at the same time

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Staying out of both Cold War military blocs while taking an active, independent stand on world issues. Non-alignment meant not joining either military alliance, but India spoke up actively on decolonisation, disarmament and peace. It was neither isolationism (withdrawal) nor neutrality (staying out of every war), and it did not mean joining both blocs.

questions.stem_md: Jawaharlal Nehru shaped India's early foreign policy because, besides being Prime Minister, he also held the post of

options.text_md: President
Chief Justice
Foreign Minister
Chief of the Army Staff

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Foreign Minister. Nehru was both Prime Minister and Foreign Minister from 1947 until his death in 1964, so he played a central role in setting foreign-policy goals.

questions.stem_md: Which of these was NOT one of the main objectives of India's foreign policy under Nehru?

options.text_md: Joining a military alliance to gain quick economic aid
Preserving the sovereignty won after a long struggle
Protecting territorial integrity
Promoting rapid economic development

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Joining a military alliance to gain quick economic aid. The three objectives usually listed are sovereignty, territorial integrity and economic development, pursued through non-alignment. Joining an alliance is the opposite of non-alignment.

questions.stem_md: Imagine a newly independent country in 1956 that refuses to join any military pact, criticises one superpower's action on one issue and the other superpower's action on another, and takes aid from both for its dams and steel plants. Which policy is it following?

options.text_md: Isolationism
Neutrality
Membership of a bloc
Non-alignment

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Non-alignment. Judging each issue on its merits, keeping out of pacts and dealing with both sides is non-alignment. Isolationism would mean staying out of world affairs; neutrality would mean taking no position; bloc membership would mean joining a pact.

questions.stem_md: India called an Asian Relations Conference in March 1947 and later supported the freedom struggle of Indonesia against Dutch rule. These steps show India's commitment to

options.text_md: joining the Western bloc
Afro-Asian unity and decolonisation
building a nuclear arsenal
a policy of isolation

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Afro-Asian unity and decolonisation. Both steps aimed at solidarity among Asian and African peoples and an end to colonial rule. Neither involved joining a bloc, nuclear weapons or isolation.

questions.stem_md: When the Janata Party government came to power in 1977, what did it say about non-alignment?

options.text_md: It would follow genuine non-alignment, correcting what it saw as a tilt towards the Soviet Union
It would give up non-alignment and join a military alliance
It would withdraw India from the United Nations
It would stop all relations with neighbouring countries

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** It would follow genuine non-alignment, correcting what it saw as a tilt towards the Soviet Union. The Janata government announced "genuine non-alignment", reflecting criticism that earlier policy had leaned towards the USSR; it kept the policy itself. It did not join an alliance, leave the UN or cut off neighbours.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Non-alignment was not a policy of running away from world affairs.

**Reason (R):** India took an active part in mediating international disputes and in campaigns against colonialism and for disarmament.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: India's active role in world affairs is exactly why non-alignment cannot be called "running away".

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** After independence India received economic help from both the USA and the USSR.

**Reason (R):** The Non-Aligned Movement held its first summit at Belgrade in 1961.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both statements are true, but R does not explain A. India's aid from both sides followed from its policy of not joining either bloc; the date and place of the first NAM summit do not explain it.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Non-alignment means the same as isolationism.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** Isolationism means keeping away from world affairs. Non-alignment means keeping out of military blocs while playing an active part in world politics.

questions.stem_md: The Afro-Asian conference held in 1955, which prepared the ground for the Non-Aligned Movement, met in the Indonesian city of ___.
questions.solution_md: The conference met at Bandung in April 1955.

questions.stem_md: Match each foreign-policy event in India's history with the year in which it took place.

options.text_md: Asian-African conference at Bandung
First summit of the Non-Aligned Movement
Agreement signed at Tashkent after a war
Treaty of Peace, Friendship and Cooperation with the USSR

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(s), (d)–(q). Bandung 1955; Belgrade summit 1961; Tashkent Agreement January 1966; Indo-Soviet Treaty August 1971.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between non-alignment and neutrality as foreign-policy positions.
questions.solution_md: Define each term and bring out the contrast between passivity and independent activity.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Neutrality** means staying **out of wars** and taking **no side** in disputes.
2. **Non-alignment** means not joining **military blocs**, but taking an **active, independent position** on each issue, and even mediating or helping in crises.

marking_scheme.step: Non-alignment explained as active and independent

questions.stem_md: Name the objectives that Nehru's foreign policy aimed to secure, and the means chosen for them.
questions.solution_md: Three objectives and the strategy of non-alignment.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Objectives:** to preserve the **hard-won sovereignty**, to protect **territorial integrity**, and to promote **rapid economic development**.
**Means:** the strategy of **non-alignment**, keeping out of the Cold War blocs.

questions.stem_md: Why did India choose non-alignment rather than joining one of the Cold War blocs? Give three reasons.
questions.solution_md: Three reasons: sovereignty, development, and peace or disarmament.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Independence of decision:** after a long freedom struggle, India wanted to decide each issue **on its merits**, not on a bloc leader's instructions.
2. **Development needs:** staying out of blocs let India seek **aid and technology from both sides** for its plans.
3. **Peace:** India believed that blocs and an **arms race** threatened world peace; by staying out it could work for **disarmament** and help mediate between the two sides.

marking_scheme.step: Aid and development from both sides

questions.stem_md: Some argue that non-alignment lost its meaning after the Cold War ended. Give one argument for this view and two against it.
questions.solution_md: A balanced answer: one argument on each side as asked, linked to the end of bipolarity.

answer.model_answer_md:
**For:** with only **one superpower** after 1991, there were no longer **two blocs** to stay away from.
**Against:** (1) the core idea, **independent decision-making** in national interest, still applies whatever the balance of power; (2) developing countries still need a **common voice** on trade, debt, climate and reform of international institutions, which a non-aligned grouping can provide.

questions.stem_md: Explain the main features of India's policy of non-alignment under Nehru. How did it serve India's interests in the 1950s?
questions.solution_md: Three features and two ways the policy served India, with examples.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Out of military blocs:** India did not join the US-led or the Soviet-led alliances.
2. **Active, not passive:** it took **independent stands** on each issue and helped **mediate**, so it was not isolationism or neutrality.
3. **Against colonialism and racism:** it supported **Afro-Asian unity** (Asian Relations Conference 1947, Bandung 1955) and freedom movements.
4. **Interests served:** it protected **sovereignty** and let India obtain **aid and technology from both sides** for planned development.
5. **Standing:** it gave a newly independent, militarily weak country a **voice in world affairs**, especially through NAM from 1961.

marking_scheme.step: Sovereignty and aid from both sides

questions.stem_md: Two imagined countries sign a pact promising to respect each other's territory, never to attack each other, to stay out of each other's internal affairs and to live in peaceful coexistence. Which agreement in India's history do these terms most closely follow?

options.text_md: Panchayati Raj
Panchsheel
the Simla Agreement
the Tashkent Declaration

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Panchsheel. These are the five principles of peaceful coexistence agreed by India and China in 1954 (Panchsheel). Panchayati Raj is a local-government system, and Simla and Tashkent were agreements with Pakistan after wars.

questions.stem_md: Which event of 1959 added to tension between India and China?

options.text_md: India and China signed the Panchsheel agreement
China joined the Non-Aligned Movement
India gave political asylum to the Dalai Lama
India tested a nuclear device

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** India gave political asylum to the Dalai Lama. After an uprising in Tibet in 1959, the Dalai Lama crossed into India and was given asylum; China objected. Panchsheel dates from 1954, China was not a NAM member, and India's first test came in 1974.

questions.stem_md: The border dispute that led to the 1962 war centred mainly on which two areas?

options.text_md: The Rann of Kutch and Sir Creek
Siachen and Kargil
The Andaman Islands and Lakshadweep
Aksai Chin in the western sector and the area then called NEFA in the eastern sector

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Aksai Chin in the western sector and the area then called NEFA in the eastern sector. The two main areas were Aksai Chin (Ladakh region) in the west and the North-East Frontier Agency (today Arunachal Pradesh) in the east. The other places relate to India–Pakistan disputes or to islands with no such dispute.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following was a political consequence of the 1962 war within India?

options.text_md: The Congress lost power at the Centre in the next general election
India left the Non-Aligned Movement
India signed a military alliance with China
The Defence Minister resigned and the Nehru government faced its first no-confidence motion in the Lok Sabha

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The Defence Minister resigned and the Nehru government faced its first no-confidence motion in the Lok Sabha. V. K. Krishna Menon left the Defence Ministry and a no-confidence motion was moved in 1963; the government survived it. The Congress kept power in 1967 at the Centre, India stayed in NAM, and there was no alliance with China.

questions.stem_md: An imagined student writes: "After 1962 India decided to spend much more on its armed forces and to modernise them." Which lesson of the war does this reflect?

options.text_md: The war proved that Panchsheel had been fully successful
The war ended all border disputes for good
The war exposed weaknesses in military preparedness
The war showed that India needed no army at all

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The war exposed weaknesses in military preparedness. The 1962 setback led to a rethink of defence and higher military spending. The war did not show Panchsheel succeeding, did not end the dispute, and pointed to the opposite of needing no army.

questions.stem_md: Differences over how to view China after 1962 contributed to a split in which political party in 1964?

options.text_md: The Indian National Congress
The Communist Party of India
The Swatantra Party
The Bharatiya Jana Sangh

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The Communist Party of India. The Communist Party of India split in 1964, and the CPI(M) emerged as a separate party; differences over relations with China and the USSR were among the reasons.

questions.stem_md: An imagined Indian visitor to Beijing in 1977 notes in her diary that the Indian embassy is once again headed by a full ambassador, for the first time in many years. Which development explains this?

options.text_md: India and China had restored full diplomatic relations in 1976
India and China had just signed the Panchsheel agreement
The Simla Agreement had settled the India–China boundary
China had joined the Non-Aligned Movement

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** India and China had restored full diplomatic relations in 1976. After the 1962 war, relations were kept at a lower level until full diplomatic relations were restored in 1976. Panchsheel dates from 1954, Simla was an India–Pakistan agreement, and China was not a NAM member.

questions.stem_md: An imagined army officer writes home in late November 1962 that the guns on the frontier have suddenly fallen silent, although no treaty has been signed and no outside force has arrived. What most likely explains this?

options.text_md: A treaty had been signed at Simla
China had declared a unilateral ceasefire
The United Nations had sent peacekeeping forces
Both sides had signed the Tashkent Agreement

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** China had declared a unilateral ceasefire. The 1962 war ended when China announced a ceasefire on its own, without any treaty. Simla (1972) and Tashkent (1966) were India–Pakistan agreements, and no UN force was involved.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The 1962 war was a setback to the spirit of Panchsheel in India–China relations.

**Reason (R):** Panchsheel had committed both countries to non-aggression and peaceful coexistence.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: because Panchsheel promised non-aggression and peaceful coexistence, an armed conflict was a direct blow to it.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** India was one of the first countries to recognise the People's Republic of China.

**Reason (R):** India and China had no differences of any kind in the 1950s.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A is true: India recognised the new government soon after 1949. R is false: differences over Tibet and the boundary already existed in the 1950s.

questions.stem_md: True or false? The India–China war of 1962 ended when China declared a unilateral ceasefire.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** China announced a unilateral ceasefire in November 1962, and the fighting stopped.

questions.stem_md: Arrange these events in India–China relations in chronological order.

options.text_md: Full diplomatic relations restored
Panchsheel agreement signed
Border war (October–November)
Dalai Lama given asylum in India

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (b) → (d) → (c) → (a). Panchsheel 1954, asylum for the Dalai Lama 1959, the border war 1962, and restoration of full relations 1976.

marking_scheme.step: Complete correct sequence (all items in place)

questions.stem_md: What was Panchsheel? Name any two of its principles.
questions.solution_md: Meaning with the year, then any two principles.

answer.model_answer_md: **Panchsheel** was the set of **five principles of peaceful coexistence** in the India–China agreement of **1954**. Two principles: **mutual non-aggression** and **non-interference in each other's internal affairs** (others: respect for territory and sovereignty, equality and mutual benefit, peaceful coexistence).

questions.stem_md: How did the Tibet question affect India–China relations in the 1950s?
questions.solution_md: Link the asylum of 1959 to growing mistrust alongside the boundary issue.

answer.model_answer_md: China took control of **Tibet** in 1950, and India accepted Chinese sovereignty there. When the **Dalai Lama** fled after the 1959 uprising, India gave him **asylum**; China saw this as unfriendly, and it **deepened mistrust** just as the **border dispute** was growing.

marking_scheme.step: Effect: mistrust added to the border dispute

questions.stem_md: Explain any three effects of the 1962 war on India.
questions.solution_md: Three distinct effects: image, defence and domestic politics.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **National image and self-confidence:** the setback hurt India's standing and the prestige of its leadership at home and abroad.
2. **Defence policy:** India sharply raised **defence spending** and modernised its forces.
3. **Domestic politics:** the **Defence Minister resigned**, the government faced its **first no-confidence motion** (1963), and differences over China contributed to the **split of the CPI** in 1964.

questions.stem_md: "From Panchsheel to war in eight years." Trace India–China relations from 1949 to 1962 and assess the main reasons for the conflict.
questions.solution_md: Chronology with four stages, then a reasoned judgement on the causes.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Friendly start:** India recognised the **People's Republic** early (1949–50) and supported its seat in the UN.
2. **Panchsheel (1954):** both sides pledged **peaceful coexistence and non-aggression**.
3. **Tibet:** China's control of Tibet and India's **asylum to the Dalai Lama (1959)** created mistrust.
4. **Boundary dispute:** rival claims over **Aksai Chin** and the eastern sector (**NEFA**) hardened after 1957; talks failed.
5. **Assessment:** the war of **October–November 1962** grew mainly from the **unresolved boundary** and mistrust over Tibet; it showed that goodwill alone could not replace a **settled border** and adequate **defence preparation**.

questions.stem_md: An imagined textbook for a foreign university describes "a 1960 agreement in South Asia, reached through an international lending institution, under which two neighbours with a territorial dispute shared the waters of six rivers". Which agreement and which mediator are described?

options.text_md: The Tashkent Agreement, mediated by the Soviet Union
The Simla Agreement, mediated by the United Nations
The Panchsheel agreement, mediated by the Commonwealth
The Indus Waters Treaty, mediated by the World Bank

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The Indus Waters Treaty, mediated by the World Bank. The Indus Waters Treaty was signed in 1960 by Prime Minister Nehru and President Ayub Khan with the World Bank as mediator. Tashkent (1966) had Soviet mediation; Simla (1972) was bilateral; Panchsheel was with China.

questions.stem_md: The Tashkent Agreement of January 1966 was signed by Prime Minister Lal Bahadur Shastri and General Ayub Khan with the mediation of

options.text_md: the Soviet Union
the United States
the United Nations Secretary-General in person
Britain

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** the Soviet Union. Soviet Premier Kosygin mediated the talks at Tashkent, then in the Soviet Union.

questions.stem_md: Which development in East Pakistan led to the crisis of 1971?

options.text_md: East Pakistan voted to join India in a referendum
India and China fought a war over East Pakistan
After the Awami League won the 1970 elections, power was not handed over, and the military crackdown that followed drove millions of refugees into India
The United Nations divided Pakistan into two countries

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** After the Awami League won the 1970 elections, power was not handed over, and the military crackdown that followed drove millions of refugees into India. The Awami League under Sheikh Mujibur Rahman won the 1970 elections; the crackdown that began in March 1971 and the flood of refugees into India led to war in December. There was no referendum, no India–China war, and no UN decision to divide Pakistan.
